name: pessimistic-offline-lock
intent: Prevent conflicts between concurrent business transactions by making each one acquire an explicit, persisted lock on the data before it starts to use it, so that once work begins it is almost certain to complete without a concurrency conflict.
problem: A business transaction spans several system transactions (user think time, multiple requests), so the database cannot enforce isolation for its whole duration; where conflict between sessions is likely and a late failure is expensive, detecting conflicts only at commit makes users repeat minutes of work, while a single long-running system transaction is not an option.
context: Interactive, multi-session applications over shared persisted state: several users (or jobs) may edit the same record or aggregate, sessions last minutes to hours across requests, and the store can host a small, fast lock registry with owner, acquisition time and timeout. It is the deliberate alternative to Optimistic Offline Lock where conflicts are frequent, costly, or both.
benefits: Conflicts are avoided before the work starts: a user who cannot get the lock is told immediately instead of discovering at commit that minutes of editing are lost.
Concurrency control becomes explicit and inspectable: the lock registry answers who holds which lock and since when, which supports monitoring, user messaging and administrative release.
Once a lock is granted the business transaction can be assumed to complete, barring unrelated failures - downstream error handling does not have to model concurrent modification of the same data.
No long-running system transaction is needed: locks are application-owned records, so no database connection or transaction stays open across user think time.
Lock granularity is a design decision rather than an accident: fine-grained object locks and coarse-grained aggregate locks use the same lock manager (see Coarse-Grained Lock).
Works on an unchanged persistence mapping: unlike version-based schemes it needs no version column added to every mapped table and no changes to how entities are stored.
tradeoffs: Availability risk of the mechanism itself: an abandoned, hung or crashed session keeps its lock until a timeout or an administrator releases it, so stale locks become operational work and timeout values must be tuned (too short re-opens the conflict window, too long blocks other users).
Reduced concurrency: the chosen lock granularity becomes a serialisation point, hot aggregates queue behind one owner, and the lock registry row can itself become a contended record.

Cross-cutting plumbing: every business transaction must acquire and release through the lock manager in a consistent order, and a single forgotten acquisition silently reintroduces the lost update the pattern was meant to prevent.

Failure modes are distributed: deadlocks from inconsistent acquisition order, leases lost when a process restarts without a persisted registry, and session-identity mistakes that let one session release another's lock.

Distributed deployments multiply the problem: in-process mutexes are useless across nodes and a shared registry (database row, advisory lock, Redis) brings its own lease-expiry, partition and clock failure modes.
Lock state is shared global state in tests: multi-session scenarios, cleanup between tests and timeout behaviour are all harder to test than a pure version check.

participants.responsibility: The only interface business code uses: acquire, release and query locks for a lockable; enforces ownership, atomicity of acquisition and timeouts, and hides the storage (lock table, advisory lock) behind one API.
The domain object, aggregate or set of records that must not be edited concurrently; identified by a stable lock key (surrogate id, aggregate root id, or a derived key for a cluster).
The durable identity of the business transaction (session or user plus process identity) that owns a granted lock; the same owner must be able to re-enter its own lock across requests and release it.
The persisted lease: lockable key, owner, acquisition time and timeout - the single source of truth for who holds what, read and written inside short system transactions only.
Bounds every lease: detects expired records, releases abandoned locks, and reports or exposes them so an administrator can release a lock whose owner will never return.

use_cases: Multi-step editing wizards over one record - insurance claim adjustment, order or invoice editing - where a session lasts minutes and a commit-time conflict would discard all of it.
Allocation against a scarce shared resource: inventory reservation, seat or capacity planning, where two planners must not promise the same units.
Periodic reconciliation work where a reviewer checks out an account, ledger or reporting period and the system must show others who is working on it.
Enterprise master-data maintenance over a shared database with low write volume but very expensive conflicts (pricing tables, contracts, configuration).
Long-running operational flows where an operator explicitly checks a configuration or document out of a repository and back in when finished.

Microsoft SharePoint document libraries with required check-out: one editor can check a document out, work offline, and check it back in; use this when exclusive ownership and visible stale-checkout recovery matter.

Redis distributed locks with a TTL (including the documented Redlock pattern): a service can claim a resource with a unique token, renew within the validity window, and let expiry recover abandoned ownership; use this only when its timing and availability assumptions fit the workload.

etcd's Lock service attached to a lease: a named lock is released by Unlock or automatically when the lease expires; use this for distributed resource ownership across nodes when automatic recovery matters, not as a substitute for database transaction isolation.
avoid_when: Conflicts are rare and a retry is cheap: Optimistic Offline Lock (a Version Number checked at commit) is simpler, needs no lock registry, and does not block anyone.
The whole edit fits inside one request or system transaction: rely on ordinary database locking and isolation levels instead of adding an offline lock manager.
Data is single-writer by construction (batch pipelines, per-user or per-tenant partitions, append-only logs): there is no concurrent session to lock against.
Throughput matters more than avoiding rework, or the record is read-mostly: locking turns a read-heavy system into a queue, and a shared lock manager adds a central bottleneck.
A distributed lock service (Redis, ZooKeeper, etcd) is already part of the platform: its lease semantics are exactly this pattern, so use it rather than hand-building a lock table.
anti_patterns: Holding a database transaction (or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) open across user think time and calling it an offline lock - it holds database resources, breaks on disconnect, and dies with the connection.
Acquiring and releasing locks ad hoc in UI or controller code instead of through a lock manager, so release paths are forgotten and stale rows accumulate.
Locking far more than the business transaction needs (whole tables, or a coarse record when one row suffices) - or the reverse, locking a field whose invariants span several rows.
Taking write locks for read-only flows, converting read-heavy usage into a queue behind the lock registry.
Using an in-process mutex or thread-local flag as the lock registry in a multi-process or multi-node deployment.
design_principles: Explicit concurrency control: lock ownership is first-class persisted state, not an implicit side effect of a transaction or an in-memory flag.
Single source of truth: exactly one registry (the lock table or an equivalent lease service) owns lock state; no parallel in-memory caches of who holds what.
Separation of concerns: business logic asks the Lock Manager, the Lock Manager owns the storage, the Lockable stays ignorant of locking.
Fail-safe defaults: every lease is bounded by a timeout, ownership is verified on release, and acquisition failure is a normal, tellable outcome.
Consistent resource ordering: acquire multiple lockables in a deterministic order so concurrent business transactions cannot deadlock.
best_practices: Model locks as records (lockable, owner, acquired_at, timeout) and make acquisition atomic inside one short transaction - insert-on-missing and update-on-expired in the same unit of work.
Verify ownership on release and make release idempotent for the owner; only the owner (or the reaper) deletes a lock record.
Bound every lock with a timeout, sweep expired locks automatically, and expose stale locks for administrative release.
Acquire in a deterministic order and release in reverse; prefer one coarse lock key per business transaction over many fine-grained locks taken at different times.
Surface lock state to users (who holds it, since when) and provide a deliberate 'locked by another user' response path instead of a generic error.
Tie the owner identity to the session/user and release locks on explicit session end, but never rely on that release path alone - crashes are what timeouts are for.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Pessimistic Offline Lock and Optimistic Offline Lock, Chapter 16 (Concurrency).
